h1: Alopecia Areata: Why Patches Appear and What Stops Them
subtitle: Smooth, round patches that appear quickly. The follicle usually survives.

hero.alt: Round alopecia areata patch on the scalp with smooth skin and short fine hairs at the border
hero.caption: The patch border, at 200x.

quickAnswer: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition where the immune system interrupts follicles that are in their growth phase. The result is usually a smooth, round patch that appears over days rather than months, with skin that looks normal rather than scarred. Because the follicle itself is not destroyed, regrowth is possible even after a long patch, and hair often returns fine and light before it returns fully pigmented. Patches can also appear in the beard or eyebrows. At Nina Ross Atlanta in Sandy Springs we confirm the pattern at 200x, look at the systems that keep the immune response stirred up, and track each patch with photographs. Serving all of Metro Atlanta.
takeaways: The follicle is usually not destroyed.
Regrowth often starts fine and light.
The patch border shows whether it is active.

items.you: A smooth bald circle appeared out of nowhere
items.why: A round patch that appears over days is commonly linked to immune activity pushing many growing follicles out of their growth phase at once.
items.check: We confirm the pattern at 200x and check that the skin is intact, which separates alopecia areata from scarring conditions.

items.you: Short hairs that look like tiny commas
items.us: Exclamation mark hairs at the patch margin
items.why: Short hairs that narrow toward the scalp are commonly linked to a patch that is still active. The follicle was interrupted mid-growth.
items.check: We read the border at 200x for these tapered hairs, which tells us whether the patch is still spreading.

items.you: The skin there looks totally normal
items.why: Normal-looking skin is a good sign. It usually means the follicles are still there, resting rather than scarred.
items.check: Magnification shows whether the openings are present, which is why regrowth stays possible.

items.you: White or fine hairs coming back in
items.why: Fine, light hairs are commonly the first sign a follicle has restarted. Pigment and thickness often return later.
items.check: We photograph the same points each visit, so you can see regrowth before it shows in the mirror.

items.you: Pitting or ridges in my nails
items.us: Nail pitting associated with alopecia areata
items.why: Small pits or ridges in the nails are described alongside alopecia areata in some people, because the same immune activity can reach the nail.
items.check: Tell us about it at your visit. It is part of the systemic picture we look at beyond the scalp.

items.title: Autoimmune activity
items.text: The immune system stops recognizing the growing follicle as its own and pushes it out of the growth phase early.

items.title: Stress and illness as triggers
items.text: A major stressor or illness often sits just before the first patch. Stress can be a trigger, and it is rarely the whole cause.

items.title: Other autoimmune conditions
items.text: Thyroid disease, vitiligo and other autoimmune conditions show up more often alongside alopecia areata, which is why we look beyond the scalp.{cite:1}

Relaxers, braids, locs, weaves and heat. Share your full hair history. It is welcomed, never judged.

faq.a: The follicle is not scarred, so regrowth is possible. What we cannot tell you is the timeline, because it varies with how widespread the patches are and how long they have been active. Results not typical. Individual results will vary.

faq.q: Why did it happen so fast?
faq.a: The immune system interrupts many growing follicles at the same moment, so the hair releases together over days. It feels sudden because it is.

faq.q: Can it come back after it fills in?
faq.a: It can. Alopecia areata can return after regrowth, which is why we keep photographing the same points and look at the systems that keep the immune response stirred up.
Stress often sits just before a first patch and can act as a trigger. The underlying driver is immune activity at the follicle, so we look at both.

faq.q: Do you treat beard and eyebrow patches?
faq.a: Patches can appear in the beard or eyebrows too. Bring them to your visit and we read them the same way we read the scalp.
